title: Public Administration
summary: Learn how governments deliver services: the values of public service, ideas from bureaucracy to New Public Management, the policy cycle and performance measurement, public finance and human resources, decentralisation and local government, and accountability, ethics and e-government.
audience: Civil servants, local government staff, students of public administration and engaged citizens

body.p: Public administration is the work of turning government policies and laws into services and results for the public: running schools and clinics, collecting taxes, issuing documents, maintaining roads and regulating businesses. It is also an academic field that studies how governments are organised and managed.

list: Public organisations serve the public interest and must treat citizens equally, while businesses aim for profit and serve customers who pay.
Public bodies are accountable to parliament, courts, auditors and voters.
They work under laws on budgets, procurement, employment and information, which limit discretion.
Success is harder to measure than profit: outcomes like literacy or health take years to change.

body.p: Many African constitutions set out values for public administration, such as professionalism and ethics, efficient and economic use of resources, impartial and fair service, responsiveness to people's needs, public participation, accountability and transparency. The African Charter on Values and Principles of Public Service and Administration sets similar standards.

body.tip: Think of citizens as the people the public service exists to serve, not as an inconvenience to manage.

lessons.title: Ideas that shaped the public service

list: Bureaucracy (Max Weber): clear hierarchy, written rules, specialised roles and appointment on merit. It brings predictability and fairness, but can become slow and rigid ("red tape").
Scientific management: studying tasks to make work efficient.

New Public Management (from the 1980s): applying business methods such as performance targets, contracting out, agencies and customer focus. It aimed to improve efficiency but sometimes weakened accountability and equity.
New Public Governance: government working through networks and partnerships with civil society, communities and the private sector.
Developmental state: a capable, committed public service leading economic transformation, often linked to East Asian experience and discussed widely in Africa.

body.p: Colonial administrations were designed mainly for control and extraction, not service. After independence, African states expanded public services rapidly, then faced structural adjustment programmes in the 1980s and 1990s that cut spending and staff. Many are now rebuilding capacity for service delivery.

body.tip: No single model fits every context; good administrators adapt ideas to local realities.

steps: Agenda setting: a problem gains attention, through media, citizens, crises or political leaders.
Policy formulation: officials analyse options, costs and evidence, and consult stakeholders.
Decision-making: cabinet, parliament or councils adopt a policy or law.
Implementation: departments plan, budget, staff and deliver programmes.
Monitoring and evaluation: tracking performance and assessing whether the policy achieved its aims.
Review: adjusting, expanding or ending the policy.

body.p: Many good policies fail in implementation because of weak funding, too few skilled staff, poor coordination between departments, corruption or lack of local buy-in. Involving front-line staff and communities in design helps.

Indicators track inputs (money, staff), outputs (clinics built, textbooks delivered) and outcomes (fewer deaths, higher reading scores). If a department planned 120 new classrooms and built 96, it achieved 96 / 120 = 80% of its target, with a shortfall of 24.

body.tip: Ask "so what?" of every output: a built clinic matters only if it has staff, medicine and patients.

body.p: Public money follows a cycle: the executive prepares the budget, parliament debates and approves it, departments spend it, and the auditor-general audits the accounts and reports back to parliament. If a department budgets R500 million for a programme and spends R540 million, the overspend is 8%, which must be justified and often approved.

list: Medium-term expenditure frameworks plan spending over three years.
Public finance management laws set rules for spending, reporting and accountability.
Citizens can read budget documents; many treasuries publish citizen's budget guides.

body.p: Most services depend on public servants: teachers, nurses, clerks and engineers. Merit-based recruitment, fair pay, training, performance management and protection from political interference build a capable public service. Patronage, where jobs are given as political rewards, undermines it. If a municipality has 300 vacancies in a structure of 1500 posts, its vacancy rate is 20%, which usually slows service delivery.

body.tip: Read your country's latest auditor-general report; it shows where public money is well or poorly managed.

body.p: Decentralisation moves authority and resources from central government to lower levels. It can bring decisions closer to people, but it needs capacity, funding and accountability at local level.

list: Deconcentration: central ministries post staff to regions but keep control.
Delegation: functions are handed to semi-autonomous bodies.
Devolution: elected local or regional governments receive constitutional powers and funds, as with Kenya's counties.
Fiscal decentralisation: local governments raise their own revenue (such as property rates and market fees) and receive transfers from the centre.

body.p: Local governments often handle water, sanitation, waste collection, local roads, markets, land use planning and primary health. Ward committees and public meetings allow citizens to participate in planning and budgeting. Traditional leaders also play roles in many rural areas, especially in land administration and dispute resolution.

body.tip: Attend a local council or ward meeting; budgets and plans are often decided with very few citizens present.

list: Political accountability: ministers answer to parliament and voters.
Financial accountability: audits and public accounts committees.
Legal accountability: courts review unlawful decisions; administrative justice laws require fair procedures and reasons for decisions.
Social accountability: citizens monitor services through scorecards, social audits and community monitoring.
Ombudsmen or public protectors investigate maladministration.

body.p: Corruption, the abuse of entrusted power for private gain, diverts resources from services. Defences include asset declarations, conflict-of-interest rules, protection for whistle-blowers, transparent procurement and anti-corruption agencies.

Digital services, such as online tax filing, electronic identity, and mobile payment of fees, can cut queues and corruption. If an online system cuts processing time for a licence from 40 days to 10, the time saved is 75%. Digital services must stay accessible to people without internet access and protect personal data.

body.tip: Good public servants record decisions and reasons; clear records protect both citizens and officials.
